analysis.one_liner: Requires managed care insurers to spend at least 85% of premiums on medical care.
analysis.headline: The Managed Care Integrity Act was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and died there without ever getting a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health maintenance organizations and other managed care insurers — covering private plans, Medicaid, federal employees, the military, and Medicare Advantage plans — to devote at least 85% of every premium dollar to actual medical care, limiting administrative costs and profits to 15%. It included enforcement with civil penalties up to $100,000, suspension of new enrollment, and suspension of payments, plus solvency waivers for struggling insurers. Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced it in March 2001; it went to the Senate health committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans: private insurance customers, Medicaid managed care members, federal employees, service members and their families, and Medicare+Choice beneficiaries. A larger share of their premiums would have to go to doctors, hospitals, and care rather than overhead, marketing, and insurer profits.

how_it_helps.text: Each managed care health plan must ensure that the actuarial value of benefits provided to enrollees is at least 85% of total premium payments received from or on behalf of enrollees each contract year [S3].

Costs of running the insurer — executive compensation and fringe benefits, interest expenses, facility occupancy, and marketing — are excluded from what counts as 'benefits,' so they cannot be used to hit the 85% target [S3].

The requirement covers managed care entities in group and individual coverage, Medicaid managed care organizations, Federal Employees Health Benefits Program plans, and plans for armed forces members and their families, and is added to Medicare+Choice plans through the Social Security Act [S3].

Enforcement includes a formal complaint investigation process, corrective action plans, hearings, civil money penalties of up to $25,000 per violation ($100,000 for misrepresentation or falsified information), and for Medicare+Choice organizations, suspension of new enrollment or of payments [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Managed care insurers, whose administrative expenses and profits would be capped at 15% of premium revenue. Insurers with thin margins could apply for time-limited waivers if compliance threatened their solvency.
analysis.who_pays_short: Managed care insurers' overhead and profits

drawbacks.text: A medical spending floor does not cap premiums: an insurer could comply with the 85% rule simply by charging higher premiums as long as 85% went to care, so it restrains how money is spent but not what people pay overall [S3].
The bill includes a waiver process — renewable up to 24 months in any 36-month period — for insurers whose solvency would be jeopardized, which could let weaker companies delay compliance [S3].

Penalties are modest relative to large insurer revenues — up to $25,000 per violation, or $100,000 involving misrepresentation — and non-Medicare plans face corrective action rather than automatic contract termination [S3].

An early compliance deadline of January 1, 2002 for contract years beginning that year left insurers and state regulators less than a year to adapt, a transition cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For enrollees, the bill's benefit is real but partial: more premium dollars going to care, with enforcement teeth and a solvency safety valve. Its main limit is that it targets overhead and profit, not premium levels themselves, and the waiver system could soften the cap for financially fragile insurers. The strongest objection — that it tells insurers how to spend premiums rather than limiting what they charge — is a fair one, but limiting overhead share was a reasonable first step, and a version of this requirement (the medical loss ratio) was later written into the Affordable Care Act in 2010.

outcome.mechanism: Feinstein introduced the bill and it was read twice and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; no committee vote, no floor action, and no cosponsors ever followed, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Feinstein introduced S. 577 in the Senate on March 20, 2001 and delivered introductory remarks the same day [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on March 20, 2001 — the last action it ever received [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during the entire Congress [S4].
The HELP Committee never reported the bill, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers were better off because the bill died: no cap was placed on their administrative expenses and profits, and they kept operating without a federal 85% medical spending floor for nearly another decade until the Affordable Care Act imposed a similar medical loss ratio in 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Managed care insurers, until the ACA's 2010 MLR rule

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor on March 20, 2001

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; received the referral
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the referred bill — no markup, no report, no vote — allowing it to die without floor consideration

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party ever joined the bill and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split was recorded; the only recorded support came from its Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Managed care insurers (HMOs and other managed care entities)
industries.note: The bill caps administrative expenses and profits at 15% of premium revenue across their private, Medicaid, federal-employee, military, and Medicare+Choice lines, backed by civil penalties, enrollment suspensions, and payment suspensions. Their ability to retain overhead and profit from premiums directly came out of the value of coverage for enrollees, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's beneficiaries.

The bill amends the Social Security Act to impose the 85% requirement on Medicare+Choice plans, with enforcement through contract termination, enrollment suspension, and payment suspension. The industry's retained margin is the cost borne by beneficiaries and taxpayers.
